text borrowed from French itaccoutrerit going back to Middle French itacoutrer acoustrerit going back to Old French itacoutrerit to put in place position perhaps going back to GalloRomance itacconstrreit to sew together mend from itait prefix forming transitive verbs going back to Latin itadit etlinkadad  itconstrait sewing seam mamatcouturema  etsnote t If the etymon behind itaccoutrerit is itaccnstrreit itaccstrreit the sense development is presumably from sew together mend to prepare trim adorn The phonetic development is more difficult the assumption is that the tonic form would be itacosturit 1 singular and the weak form itnous acostronsit with the weak form being generalized throughout the paradigm The longer form is evidenced in 13thcentury itracousturerit to stitch up a wound mend a garment unless this verb is built independently on itcoustureit Such a development is possible but it has been pointed out that verbs derived from nouns in itrait tend to preserve the itit itamesurer afaiturer empasturerit though most such verbs clearly do not date back to earlier GalloRomance or Vulgar Latin An alternative explanation sees itaccoutrerit as a derivative of itcoutreit coulter blade of a plow in which case the itsit in itacoustrerit would be hypercorrection s in this position having disappeared by the 14th century but the semantic development of such a verb is hardly transparent

text Middle English itele eill ile ildeit lateral division of a church on either side of the nave usually divided from the nave by pillars borrowed from AngloFrench itele esle aile ileit wing wing of a building lateral division of a nave continental Old French iteleit wing wing of a building going back to Latin itlait wing mamatalama etsnote t The Middle English forms itile ildeit show assimilation to itile ildeit island see etlinkisle1isle1the rows on either side of the nave perhaps being thought of as isolated from the rest of the churchand effectively supplant itele eillit etc in the sixteenth century The itdit in itildeit is a secondary extrusion compare etlinkmold3mold3 In early Modern English itileit competes orthographically with a variety of other spellings as itayleaileit which appears to have regressed to the sense wing and adopted the Middle French spelling itaileit an etymologizing variant of earlier iteleit and itisleit which copies the spelling of etlinkisle1isle1 The now standard spelling itaisleit looks like a merger of itaileit and itisleit Samuel Johnson enters itaisleit in his dictionary 1755 with some reluctance Thus the word is written by Joseph Addison but perhaps improperly since it seems deducible only from either itaileit a wing or italleit a path and is therefore to be written itaileit As Johnson was likely aware itaisleit had developed a broadened sense passage between pews in the middle of a church that copies a now outofuse sense of etlinkalley1alley1 The still broader extensions passage between seats in a train bus or airplane and space between rows of items in a department store or supermarket first appeared in American English

alchymiait transmutation of base metals into gold the philosophers stone borrowed from Arabic italkmiyit from italit the  itkmiyit art of transmuting base metals borrowed perhaps via Syriac itkmiyit from Late Greek itchyme chmeit of uncertain origin etsnote t The Greek form itchymeait would appear to be a derivative of an unattested verb itchymeeinit to pour cast fuse compare Late Greek itchmeusisit alloy itself a derivative of itchmait with short ityit fluid ingot bar etymologically something poured a derivative of itch chenit to pour shed but probably influenced in form by itchmsit animal or plant fluid as a direct derivative from itchmait would be itchymateeinit see etlinkchymechyme etlinkchylechyle etlinkfound5found5 Though this etymology would appear relatively satisfactory the existence of a variant itchmeit which in vernacular Byzantine pronunciation would not have differed from itchymeit has led to speculation of another origin It has been recognized since at least JeanFranois etlinkchampollionChampollionb itLgypte sous les Pharaonsit tome premier Paris 1814 pp 109110 that itchmeit has a striking resemblance to itChmit a name for Egypt used by Plutarch in De Iside et Osiride itMoraliait 364c Egypt moreover which has the blackest of soils they call by the same name as the black portion of the eye itChmit This word is clearly adapted from the Coptic name for Egypt itkmiit a descendant of ancient Egyptian itkmtit a name for the Nile valley taken to be a derivative of itkmit black Other sources also point to an association of alchemy and Egypt Zosimos of Panopolis active around 300 AD himself a native of late Hellenistic Egypt and an early alchemical writer connects itchmeit with Egyptian metal workers who he claims enriched their rulers by secret methods of extracting gold from sand Zosimos drew the word itchymechmeit from itChmosit also itChms Chmsiteither a person or a bookbut this is likely a backformation Byzantine chroniclers as John of Antioch seventh century refer to an edict of the Roman emperor Diocletian that ordered the burning of Egyptian books dealing with the itchmeit of gold and silver so that the Egyptians could not enrich themselves and thus be emboldened to rise against Roman rule see M Berthelot itLes origines de lalchemieit Paris 1885 pp 22 72 also itSuda On Lineit Adler number chi 280 evidence for such an edict contemporary with Diocletian does not appear to exist Whether the Egyptian etymology of itchymechmeit should completely displace the Greek or if both have some validity is still an undecided issue  For the distinction in sense after ca 1700 between italchemyit and itchemistryit see the note at etlinkchemistchemist

Medieval Latin itamalgamait has been the subject of speculation since at least the nineteenth century with no conclusive results The orientalist Marcel Devic itDictionnaire tymologique des mots franais dorigine orientaleit Paris 1876 based on a supposed variant italgameit constructed an Arabic source which he rendered as itamal aljamaait with itamalit translated as practice opposed to theory work pratique uvre and itjamaait as conjunction meeting conjonction runion perhaps as an alteration of itmujmait the whole meaning the act of consummating a marriage lacte de consommation du mariage This according to Devic would be an appropriate alchemical metaphor for the joining of mercury with another metal His etymology has been accepted in the twentieth century by the itFranzsisches etymologisches Wrterbuchit and itTrsor de la langue franaiseit The difficulty with this hypothesis howeveras already noted by the itOxford English Dictionaryit in 1884is that no such collocation has ever been located in an Arabic text A genuine Arabic predecessor of itamalgamait was pointed out by Julius Ruska in an alchemical text that he entitles Book of the Missive of Jafar aldiq on the Science of Art and the Noble Stone Buch des Sendschreibens afar aldiqs ber die Wissenschaft der Kunst und des edlen Steins in itArabische Alchemisten II afar aldiq der sechste Immit Heidelberg 1924 pp 7273 The word used is itmuljamit while the process of amalgamating is itiljamit Ruska notes that itmuljamit in the sense amalgam is also found in the Arabic dictionary itLisn alArabit by Ibn Manr Since the word cannot be parsed as the derivative of an Arabic root that is at all semantically apt Ruska returns to the idea that it is a borrowing of Greek itmlagmait emollient also in Latin texts poultice hypothesizing that it was borrowed as a medical and alchemical term via a Syriac intermediary The argument against this conjecture has been that the semantic fit is poor as a word meaning emollient or poultice has little evident connection to mercury alloys Hence if the Greek hypothesis is correct a significant element still appears to lack elucidation

text Middle English itenbuschenit to place in hiding in order to attack by surprise to hide oneself in order to attack by surprise borrowed from AngloFrench itembuscherit to place in the woods in order to attack by surprise conceal lie in wait to attack by surprise also continental Old French Normandy  Picardy itembuschierit Picard dialect itembusquierit from itemit etlinkemen1  itbuscherit verbal derivative of Picard itbus buscit forest grove going back to Old Low Franconian itbskait going back to Germanic ablaut variant of itbuskait bush thicket mamatbush1ma etsnote t Forms with initial itamit instead of itemit which first appear in the noun in the sixteenth century and the verb in the seventeenth century are of uncertain origin Given the earlier use in nouns their appearance may be a byproduct of shift of stress to the initial syllable The suggestion in the itOxford English Dictionaryit third edition that the change is due to association with etlinkambageambage does not seem very likely  The meaning forest grove attached to itbskait whence the Picard masculine noun itbus buscit receded early before a GalloRomance derivative itbuskait a reformation of the Germanic etymon as a neuter collective plural noun taken as feminine whence Old French itbuscheit piece of firewood French itbcheit This new formation also with results in Occitan and Upper Italian dialects represents a sense shift from bush thicket to wood collected for a fire to split piece of wood splinter For a detailed discussion of Romance and Germanic outcomes of itbskait see Johannes Hubschmied Romanischgermanische Wortprobleme I Zur Geschichte von bois bche mit Bercksichtigung der Ortsnamen itVox Romanicait Band 29 1970 pp 11416 Within the framework of Germanic and IndoEuropean ablaut patterns as now understood a lengthened grade itbskait is questionable and one might have to appeal to variation of expressive vocabulary within Germanic Hubschmid however works within J Pokornys framework where an IndoEuropean root with a very general meaning and form itbeu bsuphsupeu bsuphsupeuit to swell is subject to an indefinite number of ablaut variants and root extensions

text Middle English itanfeld anefelt anvelt anvyllit going back to Old English itanfealtit and itanefilt anelfilteit going back to Germanic itanafaltait and itanafeltjait whence also from the first Old High German itanafalzit anvil and from the second Middle Dutch itaenvilte anevilteit from itanait on and itfalta feltjait nominal derivatives from itfaltanit taken to mean to strike beat mamatfelt1ma etsnote t The word itanvilit was originally a deverbal compound meaning in effect the thing on which striking is done Already in Old English the makeup of the compound would have been less than transparent as a verb corresponding to the deverbal second element itfealtfiltititeit does not appear to have existed or at least is not attested Such a verb does exist in Old High German though only in extended andor specialized senses see note at etlinkfelt1felt1 Parallel to itanafaltaanafeltjait were other Germanic compounds meaning anvil itanabautait whence Middle Low German itanebt ambtit Old High German itanabzit presentday German itAmboit from itbautanit to strike beat see etlinkbeat1beat1 and itanabaltjait whence Middle Low German itnebelteit Middle Dutch itaenbeltit Dutch itaanbeeldit Old High German itanabelziit and itanabultait whence Middle Low German itnebolt amboltit Old High German itanabolzit from the verbal base behind Old English itboltit bolt arrow Old High German itbolzit bolt hot iron see etlinkbolt1bolt1 It has been suggested that all the Germanic compounds are calques on Latin itincd incsit anvil formed from itinit etlinkin2in2  itcdereit to beat strike hammer Alternatively the formation of such nouns may have been a European areal feature compare Russian itnakovlnjait anvil from itnait on and a derivative of the verb itkovtit to hammer forge BosnianCroatianSerbian itnkvanjit

text borrowed from Medieval Latin borrowed from Greek itaortit aorta bronchial tubes in plural itaortait knapsack nominal derivative from the stem of itaereinit to join attach harness of uncertain origin etsnote t The word appears earlier as Middle English itaborchi abhorti adorteit aorta comparable with Middle French itaborthiit and Medieval Latin itadortiit these forms most likely reflect Latin translation of the Arabic versions of Greek medical texts  The Greek medical term itaortit belongs to a small set of forms based on itaereinit that refer to both attachment and suspension as itrtoit was hung mchaira pr xpheos mga koulen aen rto  the knife was always hung beside the great sheath of his sworditIliadit 3 272 itaortrit belt or strap for hanging a sword or satchel and itartsit knapsack Perhaps the aorta was pictured as an organ attached to and suspended from the heart in the way a scabbard is hung from a belt Note that the verb itaereinit displays two sets of meanings that of harnessing and attachment outside of nominal derivation almost always with the prefix itsynit etlinksynsyn and of lifting or raising Whether or not these should be regarded as two verbs of distinct origin or as semantic branches of the same verb is unclear Though an IndoEuropean verb base ithinf2infuerit can be reconstructed from the Greek evidence there appear to be no definitely comparable forms outside Greek See also etlinkarteryartery etlinkmeteormeteor

text Middle English itapron aperonit alteration by misdivision of ita napronit as itan apronit of itnaproun naperon napronit borrowed from AngloFrench itnaperounit napkin for drying ones hands earlier Latinized as itnapero naperonait cloth to cover a table or other surface towel apron from itnapeit tablecloth going back to Vulgar Latin itnappait by dissimilation from Latin itmappait piece of cloth used as a towel or napkin  iteronit diminutive suffix mamatmap1 mataileronma etsnote t Although modern French retains the word itnapperonit in the sense protective piece of cloth as a table mat placed on a piece of furniture the diversification in sense that led to apron in English appears to have taken place only in AngloFrench The itMiddle English Dictionaryit records itnaproun naperonit etc only in the sense apron according to the judgment of the editors but nearly all the citations are from payment records or inventories that appear to reveal little about the meaning of the word The itAngloNorman Dictionaryit has a single citation for itnaperounit from a courtesy manual of ca 1430 where it means something like napkin Sur le naperoun voz mains suetz Ne frotez voz gencies Wipe your hands on the itnaperounit dont rub your gums Continental evidence for the word apparently does not extend before the fourteenth century The AngloFrench word is demonstrably earlier however The itDictionary of Medieval Latin from British Sourcesit first records itnaperonit in the English Close Rolls as something for which cloth was required in 1215 An entry for 1274 in the household book of Henry son of Edward I registers payment for canvas cloth purchased for covering garments of the same and for itnaperonesit in the kitchen pro x ulnis canubie emptis ad cooperiendas robas eorundem et ad naperones in coquina Here the word itnaperonesit clearly points to a kind of apron This use is confirmed by a passage from the Exchequers accounts for 1313 for canvas purchased for itnapronit made to preserve the falconers clothes while they feed the falcons pro canabo empto pro napron faciend pro salvacione pannorum falconariorum in pascendo falcones

text Middle English borrowed from Latin itaptusit fastened connected prepared in good order good at doing something suitable fitting past participle of itapio apereit to join connect of uncertain origin etsnote t Though the presumed participle itaptusit is wellattested in Latin the simple verb itapereit is known only from the lexicographical comments of the Roman grammarian Sextus Pompeius Festus Possibly related on phonetic grounds to itapereit are the verbs itcoep coepisseit to begin attested only in the perfect and itapscor apscit to seize hold of grasp obtain secure The Latin complex is conventionally linked with Sanskrit itpait and Avestan itpait has reached Sanskrit itpntiit reaches overtakes and Hittite itepziit seizes captures and itappanziit they seize from an alleged IndoEuropean verbal base ithinf1infepit seize with the perfects in Latin and Sanskrit the outcome of a reduplicated ithinf1infehinf1infopit However if the primary meaning of the Latin verb is join which appears likely cf itcpulait bond fastening from itcoapulait see etlinkcouple1couple1 then itapscit and itcoepit appear semantically too distant unless in an inchoative and middle derivative the sense join oneself to led to seize hold of obtain If itapereaptusit is unrelated to itapscit and itcoepit another possible point of relation would be Hittite ithpziit joins attaches going back to IndoEuropean ithinf2infepit This would also ease the difficulty of accounting for the vocalism itait in Latin at least in itapereit if not in itapscit

century OmahaPonca itabahuit and Kansa itaropwahit For more forms and bibliography see itHandbook of North American Indiansit vol 13 itPlainsit Washington DC 2001 pp 85961 The itHandbookit editors consider the CrowHidatsa translation of the name as ldquomany tattoosrdquo to be a folk etymology Also rejected is the supposed Pawnee source itrarapihuruit ldquoone who tradesrdquo or ittirapihuuit ldquohe trades bartersrdquo ldquothere is no evidence other than similarity of forms to support the derivationrdquo The earliest record of this ethnonym is the form itArrahpahooit which was inexplicably recorded as the selfdesignation of the Republican River Pawnee band by William Clark in his ldquoEstimate of the Eastern Indiansrdquo a tabular summary of all the Indigenous Americans east of the Rockies sent from Ft Mandan to Washington by Clark in April 1805 reproduced at the website of itThe Journals of the Lewis and Clark Expedition Onlineit The bands actual selfdesignation is itkitkahahkiit which bears no resemblance to Clarks itArrahpahooit After Clark forms comparable to itArapahoit can be found in accounts and documents of beaver trapping expeditions to the upper Missouri John Bradbury a botanical collector who accompanied the Pacific Fur Company expedition led by Wilson Price Hunt recorded the word while visiting the Arikara villages on the upper Missouri on June 16 1811 ldquo some Indians had arrived from the Chayenne nation One of these Indians was covered with a buffalo robe curiously ornamented with figures worked with split quills I understood that this robe had been purchased from the Arapahoes or Big Bead Indians a remote tribe who frequent the Rocky Mountainsrdquo itTravels in the Interior of America in the Years 1809 1810 1811it Liverpool 1817 pp 12324 A Hispanicized version of the name as itArapaosit occurs in a letter written in Spanish to authorities in Santa Fe by the fur trading entrepreneur Manuel Lisa on September 8 1812 see Herbert E Bolton ldquoNew Light on Manuel Lisa and the Spanish Fur Traderdquo itSouthwestern Historical Quarterlyit vol 17 no 1 July 1913 pp 6166 Lisas use appears to be reflected in the form itArepaosit in a journal kept by a member of one of Lisas expeditions ldquoMr Charles Sanguinette  on his return from the Arepaos in which he confirmed the sad News of the hunters he found none and was informed by the Arepaos that 3 of them were Killed by the Blackfeet rdquo December 13 1812 entry in itJournal of a FurTrading Expedition on the Upper Missouri 18121813it edited by Stella M Drumm Missouri Historical Society 1920 p 101 the unsigned manuscript is attributed by the editor to John C Luttig the clerk of the expedition Clark in the same document recorded the selfdesignation of what would become the southernmost band of the Arapaho the Nawathinehena as itNimiousinit this linguistically quite divergent band would later merge with the more northerly Hinanaeina and adopt their language Note that in 1805 the five bands now counted as Arapaho would not have struck outsiders as a clear ethnic or political unit

text Middle English itardaunt ardentit burning fiery passionate borrowed from Middle French itardent ardantit going back to Old French borrowed from Latin itardent ardensit burning fiercely hot shining eager passionate from present participle of itardreit to burn emit light or flame be fiercely hot be violently excited be eager derivative of itridus rdusit dry waterless mamataridma etsnote t The assumption here is that the initial long vowel of itridusit is shortened in itardreit though this is uncertain Ernout and Meillet in itDictionnaire tymologique de langue latineit marked it as long though M Leumann in itLateinische Laut und Formenlehreit considered it to have been shortened Although derivation of itardreit from itridusit seems likely on a morphological basis the semantic relation is anomalous as the verb is not a stative derivative of the adjectivethe verb itrreit to be dry parched already serves that function The noun itardorit is similarly anomalous Most other stative verbs in itreit paired with adjectives in itidusit have a corresponding abstract noun ending in itr orit originally its sit but the pair itridusrreit lacks a corresponding noun itrorit The derivative itardorit does not provide it as it means burning fierce heat not dryness though heat produces dryness the implicit semantic connection

text borrowed from New Latin itarillusit going back to Medieval Latin grape seed borrowed from a central or southern Italian dialectal form as Lazio dialect Subiaco itaruit grape seed 16thcentury Sicilian itarilluit going back to Vulgar Latin itarllusit of obscure origin etsnote t See itLessico etimologico italianoit vol 3 columns 115155 The inclusion of itarillusit in the itCorpus Glossariorum Latinorumit and hence the itThesaurus Linguae Latinaeit is misleading as the marginal note in the manuscript that uses the word Biblioteca Ambrosiana C 243 is later than the manuscript itself 10thllth centurieshence a Late Latin date for the word is not supportable and the Medieval Latin instances see itMittellateinisches Wrterbuch Dictionary of Medieval Latin from British Sourcesit are clearly latinizations of a vernacular word Judging by the medieval attestation in glossaries and in works of both a medical and botanical nature the itLessicoit suggests that the word may have first circulated in the Salerno school of medicine Schola Medica Salernitana Such a source corresponds well with the range of its outcomes in Romance limited to Italian dialects from Lazio and Abruzzi south through Sicily The date at which itarillusit became a technical botanical term is uncertain It was familiar to Linnaeus who uses it in a somewhat more general sense tunica propria exterior seminis sponte secedens the exterior coat of the seed proper dropping off of its own accord itPhilosophia botanicait Stockholm 1751 p 54

text Middle English itaraynen areynen arreynenit to ask a question ask someone a question interrogate rebuke in law call upon to answer an accusation borrowed from AngloFrench itarener araisner arrenerit to speak to ask questions of call to account in law call upon to answer an accusation going back to Vulgar Latin itadratinreit from Latin itadit etlinkadad  Vulgar Latin itratinreit to speak converse verbal derivative of Latin itratin ratiit reckoning calculation explanation early Medieval Latin also justification dispute discussion speech mamatreason1ma etsnote t The spoken Latin form itadratinreit gave rise to two paradigms in medieval French one based on stress on the stem as in first person singular itjaraisoneit another based on stress on the ending as in second person plural itvous araisniezit In AngloFrench these developed into two more or less distinct verbs itarenerit and itaraisunerit with only partial semantic overlap the legal sense belonging predominantly to itarenerit The verb itaraisunerit was taken into Middle English as itaresounenit to address ask a question with present with an accusation as a very infrequent meaning it appears to have dropped from use after the sixteenth century In modern standard French only the tonic form itarraisonerit survives to judge by its inclusion in FrenchEnglish dictionaries Larousse OxfordHachette the most current meaning is to board and inspect an airplane or ship The itgit in English itarraignit which first turns up in the early sixteenth century has no evident etymological justification

itasteroidit in its current sense was by the astronomer William etlinkherschelHerschelb in the paper Observations on the two lately discovered celestial Bodies Read May 6 1802 itPhilosophical Transactions of the Royal Society of Londonitit for the year MDCCCIIit part II 1802 p 22829 With this intention therefore I have endeavoured to find out a leading feature in the character of these new stars and as planets are distinguished from the fixed stars by their visible change of situation in the zodiac and comets by their remarkable comas so the quality in which these objects differ considerably from the two former species is that they resemble small stars so much as hardly to be distinguished from them even by very good telescope From this their asteroidical appearance if I may use that expression therefore I shall take my name and call them itAsteroidsit reserving to myself however the liberty of changing that name if another more expressive of their nature should occur The coinage and reception of this word have been examined in exhaustive detail by Clifford J Cunningham in Discovery of the origin of the word itasteroidit and the related terms itasteroidal planetoid planetkin planetuleit and itcometoidit itStudia Etymologica Cracoviensiait vol 20 2015 pp 4762 Cunningham establishes that the word itasteroidit was suggested by the classicist Charles Burney 17571817 through the mediation of his father the musician and composer Charles Burney 17261814 a close friend of William Herschel Left unanswered however and probably unaswerable is the question of how Burney came upon the word did he derive it himself from Greek itastrit star and the English suffix itoidit already somewhat productive or did he consult a Greek dictionary Note that Greek itasteroeidsit glossed sternartig starlike not a wellattested word is entered in Johann Gottlob Schneiders itKritisches griechischdeutsches Handwrterbuchit ZllichauLeipzig 1797 probably the most comprehensive dictionary that would have been available to Burney As is clear from Herschels words the choice of itasteroidit was determined by their visual resemblance to stars however inappropriate it might seem to twentyfirst century astronomy Cunningham points out that itplanetoidita better descriptive term as an asteroid resembles a planet more than a starwas actually used as Italian and French itplanetoidesit by Giuseppe Piazzi who spotted Ceres the first asteroid to be discovered Independently of Piazzi itplanetoidit was also arrived at by Henry Brougham editor of the itEdinburgh Reviewit who acidly criticized Herschels choice of itasteroidit Why not for instance call them itConcentric Cometsit or itPlanetary Cometsit or itCometary Planetsit Or if a single term must be found why may we not coin such a phrase as itPlanetoidit or itCometoidit itEdinburgh Reviewit January 1803 p 430 Whatever its defects the term itasteroidit has nonetheless become thoroughly established in astronomy

text Latin itaudit stem of itaudreit to hear  etlinkoo  etlinkmetermeter mamataudible1ma etsnote t The word itaudiometerit was used for a device developed by the British inventor David Edward Hughes 18311900 described by him in On an InductionsCurrent Balance and Experimental Researches made therewith itProceedings of the Royal Society of Londonit no 196 May 15 1879 vol 29 pp 5665 Though the word is used by Hughes p 58 it was coined by the British physician Benjamin Ward Richardson 182896 who concludes a report following Hughes article in the same journal Some Researches with Professor Hughes New Instrument for the Measurement of Hearing the Audiometer pp 6570 with the following  the world of science  is under a deep debt of gratitude to Professor Hughes for his simple and beautiful instrument which I have christened the audimeter or less correctly but more euphoniously the audiometer Presumably Richardson felt that itiit was a more Latinate linking vowel than itoit following a Latin element though the precedents in classical Latin for 4thconjugation verbs in compounds are limited but cf the derivatives itfulcmen fulcmentumit prop support from itfulcreit to support and the hapax in Petronius itfulcipediaitwith ititone supported by a foot But itoit as a universal linking element in GrecoLatin compounds was most likely becoming general usage in the 19th century

text perhaps blend of etlinkautomatic1automatic1 and etlinkoperationoperation etsnote t The coinage of this word has been attributed to the Ford Motor Company executive Delmar S Harder 18921973 who in the period 194748 was a vice president of manufacturing In the third volume of a history of Ford by Allan Nevins and Frank Ernest Hill itFord Decline and Rebirth 19331962it New York 1963 p 354 the following account is given At a staff meeting in 1947 Harder suggested a new department to study the efficient handling of materials Harder groped for a name the Automated Handling Department he suggested then better still the Automation Department This seems to have been the first significant appearance of the word Later Harder dated its use back to 1936 when he was at Grand Rapids with General Motors By the diligent efforts of Ford publicity men and his own impressive accomplishments Harder came to be known as the father of automation John Diebold of the Harvard Business School also claims to have invented the word automation but seems to have done so according to the Ford version a few days later than Harders use in 1947 Unfortunately Nevins and Hill give no exact source for this story though according to a later endnote Harder was interviewed by them on November 12 1959 An early printed instance of itautomationit is in an article in the trade journal itAmerican Machinistit Ford Handles by Automation by Rupert Le Grand vol 92 no 22 October 21 1948 pp 10722 It is not certain that John Diebold an early writer on automation ever claimed to have coined the word at any rate in 1947 when the Automation Department was formed at Ford Diebold who was born in 1926 was an undergraduate at Swarthmore and unlikely to have been in a position to introduce the word See also the note at etlinkautomateautomate

text borrowed from French itaxiologieit from Greek itaxait worth value noun derivative from feminine of itxiosit worth equal of an equal status  French itoit etlinkoo  itlogieit etlinklogylogy mamataxiomma etsnote t The term was apparently introduced by the German philosopher Eduard von Hartmann 18421906 in Laxiologie et ses divisions itRevue philosophique de la France et de ltrangerit quinzime anne No 11 novembre 1890 pp 46679 A note at the end of the article states that the translation presumably from German to French was by M Alexandre Keller In a footnote to the word in the title of the article Hartmann states that Le mot itaxiologieit est tir du grec  valuation valeur littralement pese du grec  conduire guider charrier  The word itaxiologyit is taken from Greek itaxait valuation value literally weighing from Greek itgait to lead guide carry  In fact Greek itaxait does not mean weighingthis is an artificial sense imposed on the word based on its presumed etymology see note at etlinkaxiomaxiom Additionally the infinitive of the Greek verb is itgeinit and it is unclear what Hartmann had in mind by citing itgait which does not correspond to any form of the verb

text etlinkaxialaxial  etlinkon2on2 etsnote t The name itaxionit was introduced by the American physicist Stephen Weinberg born 1933 in A New Light Boson itPhysical Review Lettersit vol 40 no 4 January 23 1978 p 233 and by American physicist Frank Wilczek born 1951 in Problems of Strong itPit and itTit Invariance in the Presence of Instantons itPhysical Review Lettersit vol 40 no 5 p 279 In an article in the online journal itQuantait Times Almost Irreversible Arrow January 7 2016 Frank Wilczek explained the coinage as follows A few years before in 1977 a supermarket display of brightly colored boxes of a laundry detergent named Axion had caught my eye It occurred to me that axion sounded like the name of a particle and really ought to be one So when I noticed a new particle that cleaned up a problem with an axial current I saw my chance I soon learned that Steven Weinberg had also noticed this particle independently He had been calling it the Higglet He graciously and I think wisely agreed to abandon that name Thus began a saga whose conclusion remains to be written

text borrowed from Louisiana French earlier itbayouqueit perhaps borrowed from early Choctaw itbayokit whence Choctaw itbokit creek river etsnote t A Choctaw source for the word has been claimed since Albert Gatschet itA Migration Legend of the Creek Indiansit vol 1 Philadelphia 1884 p 113   the Chahta word for a smaller river or river forming part of a delta is byuk contraction bk and occurs in Boguechito Bokhumma etc However itbayukit is apparently not attested in 19th20th century Choctaw and the notion that Choctaw itbokit creek river is a contraction of itbayukit is simply Gatschets conjecture The earliest attestation of the word is apparently in the memoirs of the French carpenter Andr Pnicaut writing in 1723 A cinq lieues plus loin en tournant tousjours  la gauche sur le lac on trouve une eau dormante que les Sauvages appellent Bayouque  Five leagues farther always turning to the left along the lake shore one comes to a stagnant body of water that the Indians call bayouque see Pierre Margry editor itDcouvertes et tablissements des Franais dans lOuest et dans le Sud de lAmrique Septentrionale 16141754 Mmoires et Documents Originauxit 5 partie Paris 1887 p 385 translated by Richebourg McWilliams in itFleur de Lys and Calumet Being the Pnicaut Narrative of French Adventure in Louisianait University of Alabama Press 1981 1953 It should be noted that Pnicaut who was resident in Louisiana from 1699 to 1721 was not the most reliable recorder of what the local Indians actually spoke he also avers that itmaringouinit mosquito gnat and itsagamitit stew or soup made with hominy are the words used for these things by the local Indians though both are in fact imports into North American French from other parts of the New World Margry op cit pp 384 386 However insecure the Choctaw etymology of itbayouqueit it is accepted in volume 14 Southeast of the itHandbook of North American Indiansit Smithsonian Institution 2004 according to which the ethnic name itBayacchytoit recorded in 1699 by Pierre Le Moyne dIberville seems to be early Choctaw itbayoktoit big bayou  which in its later form itboktoit is preserved in the name of Bogue Chitto a tributary of the Pearl River   p 175

itainait goes back to itaniit with itiit the Greek outcome of an IndoEuropean formation called the itdevit inflection from its designation in Sanskrit grammar with alternating stems in IndoEuropean terms itihinf2infiehinf2infit The extended form itniit is used in Greek in a group of words characterized by P Chantraine as vocabulaire noble forming feminine counterparts to masculine nouns hence itthainait goddess itthesit god itptniait lady queen itpsisit husband itdspoinait mistress of the house itdesptsit master see itLa formation des noms en grec ancienit pp 10309 With this function there are clear parallels in other IndoEuropean languages with much reformationcompare Sanskrit itpatnit lady Old Church Slavic itbogyniit goddess Latin itregnait queen Old Irish itrgainit On this basis the itrebroussementit literally brushing the wrong way itainait is used in words for things of very low regard At this point the suffix seems to intersect with substratal vocabulary as a number of the relevant derivatives if not marked with other features of such vocabulary allude to the Mediterranean natural world itlkainait shewolf itlkosit wolf itkprainait wild boar loose woman itkprosit boar Fixed Starsit by the 10thcentury Persian astronomer Abd alRaman alf The word itjawzit perhaps a derivative of itjawzit center middle was originally a name for Gemini but applied also to Orion after Arabic astronomy incorporated Ptolemaic star nomenclature The phrase ityad aljawzit underwent a curious transformation in the Latin edition of the Alfonsine Tables a set of astronomical tables compiled by order of the Castilian king Alfonso X in ca 126376 printed in Venice by Johannes Lucilius Santritter in 1492 it emerged as itBeldelgenzeit with itnit for ituit an extraneous itlit and most remarkably an initial itbit The itbit is likely a misreading as itbit of the Arabic letter ityit as the two letters differ only in the number of dots written below them On the basis of this erroneous armpit in Scaligers edition of the itAstronomiconit of Marcus Manilius Leiden 1600 p 482 Ludewig Ideler corrected Scaligers itbit to the singular itibit armpit in itUntersuchungen ber den Ursprung und die Bedeutung der Sternnamenit Berlin 1809 p 223 the basis of an etymology that is still commonly cited Scaligers itBetelgeuzeit was taken up in Johann Bayers itUranographiait Ulm 1603 an influential star atlas that introduced the naming of stars by Greek or Latin letters followed by the Latin genitive of the constellation name From this beginning forms of the name itBetelgeuseit circulated into text variant of itblenkit going back to Middle English itblenkenit to shine gleam turn pale and to move suddenly or sharply change direction evade mislead perhaps going back to Germanic itblinkanit nasal present based on preGermanic itbleikit the base of itblkanit to shine or alternatively if itblenkit is primary a derivative from the base of itblankait bright white without color mamatbleach1 matblank1ma etsnote t In Middle English the verbs itblenkenit and itblenchenit see etlinkblench1blench1 cannot be easily separated by sense The variants with itkit to judge by citations in itMiddle English Dictionaryit are less common though the preterit itbleynteit might represent either variant There are only a few Middle English forms with itiit rather than iteit two of them from Robert Mannyng of Brunnes itHandlyng Synneit in the senses open the eyes while waking up and lead astray otherwise itblinkit is rare before the seventeenth century  Middle English itblenkenit is paralleled by Middle Dutch itblenken blinkenit to shine Middle Low German itblenkenit to shine also to make bright or clean The late appearance of these verbs in Germanic as well as the divergences in meaning make it difficult to divine the original situation moreover the expressive nature of verbs having the do with effects of light compare in English itsparkle twinkle glitterit etc favors multiplication of variants If iteit is the primary vowel in English and the continental dialects itiit may be explained as either raising before a nasal or neutralizing of the distinction as in modern southern American English The meanings evade mislead can be seen as a causative of to shine by way of a sense deceive by means of light bedazzle It is harder to explain the merger of presumed causative forms with stative forms however
